title: The 10 Best Circular Saws
subtitle: Ranked from live Amazon data — corded and cordless, from budget legends to pro worm drives.
intro: A circular saw is the workhorse that rips sheet goods and crosscuts framing lumber. The big choice is corded versus cordless: corded saws give you full, unlimited power for the least money and never need a battery, while cordless saws trade a little power for the freedom to cut anywhere. DEWALT and SKIL dominate this category on Amazon, and a couple of names — the SKIL 5280 and the SKILSAW worm drive — are near-legendary. Two things to watch: most cordless saws sell as a bare tool (no battery), and plenty of cheap "mini" saws in the results can't actually cut through a 2x4. Each pick below says exactly what it is.

products.name: DEWALT DWE575SB 7-1/4" Corded Circular Saw (electric brake)
products.verdict: The best all-around saw here. At 4.8 stars it's the highest-rated, and the electric brake, 57° bevel, and light 8.8 lb corded body make it the one most people should own. The SKIL below is cheaper, but this is the better tool.
pros: 4.8 stars over 5,000+ reviews
Electric brake stops the blade fast when you release the trigger
Light (8.8 lb) with a 57° bevel and full corded power
cons: Costs more than twice the budget SKIL
Corded — you're tied to an outlet or cord
No laser guide

products.name: SKIL 5280-01 15 Amp 7-1/4" Corded Circular Saw
products.verdict: The value legend — and the single highest-scoring saw on this list. 14,000 reviews at 4.7 stars, full 15-amp power, a laser guide, all for around $70. If you want the most saw per dollar, this is it.
pros: Most-reviewed saw here by far — 14,140 ratings at 4.7 stars
Full 15-amp corded power for under $70
Single-beam laser guide included
cons: No electric brake
Basic build vs the DEWALT and SKILSAW
Corded only

products.name: SKILSAW SPT77WML-01 15 Amp 7-1/4" Worm Drive Saw
products.verdict: The pro's saw. A worm-drive gearbox puts more torque to the blade for cutting wet lumber and long rips, and the magnesium body keeps it to a light-for-a-worm-drive 11.5 lb. Overkill for a bookshelf; perfect if you frame houses.
pros: Worm-drive torque powers through wet and thick stock
Lightweight magnesium build (11.5 lb for a worm drive)
Ships with a Diablo carbide blade; 4.8 stars
cons: Most expensive saw on the list
Heavier and longer than a sidewinder
More saw than casual DIY needs

products.name: DEWALT DCS391B 20V MAX 6-1/2" Cordless Circular Saw (tool only)
products.verdict: The go-anywhere pick, and the best-selling cordless saw here (11,000+ reviews). Cut where there's no outlet — just remember it's a bare tool, so you need a DEWALT 20V battery.
pros: Cordless freedom with 11,141 reviews at 4.6 stars
5,150 rpm and a 0-50° bevel
Runs on the huge DEWALT 20V MAX battery lineup
cons: Tool only — no battery or charger
6-1/2" blade cuts shallower than a 7-1/4"
Less sustained power than a corded 15-amp saw

products.name: Makita 5007F 7-1/4" Corded Circular Saw
products.verdict: A pro-grade corded classic. The 5007F is smooth, fast (5,800 rpm), and built to last, with twin LED lights on the cut line. A favorite of tradespeople who don't want a worm drive.
pros: Smooth, fast 5,800 rpm 15-amp motor
Built-in LED lights on the blade line
Long-running Makita reliability
cons: Pricier than the SKIL for similar cutting
No electric brake
Corded only

products.name: Milwaukee M18 2630-20 6-1/2" Cordless Circular Saw (tool only)
products.verdict: The cordless pick for people already on Milwaukee M18. Solid and well-balanced for a bare tool; not the fastest, but it taps into one of the best battery platforms out there.
pros: Runs on the excellent Milwaukee M18 battery system
0-50° bevel, 4.6 stars
Well-balanced for one-handed control
cons: Tool only — no battery or charger
3,500 rpm is on the slower side
Only worth it if you own M18 batteries

products.name: SKILSAW SPT67WL-01 15 Amp 7-1/4" Sidewinder Saw
products.verdict: Worm-drive power in a lighter sidewinder body. The Dual-Field motor runs cooler under load, and the 56° bevel is generous. A great middle ground between the budget SKIL and the full worm drive.
pros: Dual-Field motor stays cooler on long cuts
Big 56° bevel capacity
4.8 stars, lighter than a worm drive
cons: Fewer reviews than the big sellers
No brake or laser
Corded only

products.name: Skil 5080-01 13 Amp 7-1/4" Corded Circular Saw
products.verdict: The rock-bottom price for a real 7-1/4" saw. A 13-amp motor is a touch less muscle than the 15-amp models, but for occasional cuts around the house it's hard to argue with $44 and 5,000+ reviews.
pros: Cheapest full-size 7-1/4" saw here
13-amp corded power, 5,346 reviews at 4.6 stars
Ready to use — just plug in
cons: 13 amps vs 15 on the better saws
No brake, laser, or frills
Basic build

products.name: RYOBI ONE+ P505 18V 5-1/2" Cordless Circular Saw (tool only)
products.verdict: The cheapest way into a cordless saw if you're on RYOBI ONE+. The 5-1/2" blade is light and handy for plywood, trim, and breaking down sheet goods — just not deep enough for thick stock.
pros: Very cheap for a name-brand cordless saw
Light and easy to handle at 5-1/2"
Huge RYOBI ONE+ 18V battery ecosystem
cons: Tool only — no battery or charger
5-1/2" blade limits cut depth
Not for heavy framing

products.name: GALAX PRO 20V 4-1/2" Cordless Mini Circular Saw (kit)
products.verdict: A true mini saw for one-handed jobs — plywood, paneling, PVC, laminate flooring. It ships with a battery and two blades, but know the limits: a 4-1/2" blade won't cut through a 2x4 in one pass.
pros: Comes with a battery, charger, and two blades
Light one-handed body with a laser guide
Handy for plywood, trim, and flooring
cons: 4-1/2" blade can't cut a 2x4 in a single pass
Lowest rating on the list at 4.2 stars
Not a substitute for a full-size saw

avoid.name: Bigheimer 4" "Mini Circular Saw" / Cut-Off Tool
avoid.flag: A 4" angle grinder with a saw guard — cuts 5/8" deep
avoid.verdict: This isn't a circular saw — it's a 4-inch angle grinder with a saw guard bolted on. It cuts 5/8 of an inch deep and spins at grinder speed. Wrong, and genuinely unsafe, for the work a circular saw does.
reasons: It cuts only 5/8 inch (16 mm) deep. A real circular saw cuts about 2-1/2 inches — enough to crosscut a 2x4 in one pass. At 5/8", this can't cut through standard lumber or plywood on edge at all.
It's a 4-inch angle grinder with a saw guard, and it spins at 12,000 RPM. Real circular saws run around 5,000-5,800 RPM; spinning a wood blade at grinder speed is a kickback and injury risk.
No-name "Bigheimer" brand, sold tool-only (needs a DEWALT battery), and it carries the lowest star rating in the category at 3.5.
If you actually want a grinder for metal and tile, buy a grinder. If you want to cut wood, none of this tool's tricks replace a real circular saw.

buyers_guide.a: Corded saws give you unlimited full power for the lowest price and never need a battery — best for a fixed shop or long cutting sessions. Cordless saws let you cut anywhere with no cord, at a small cost in sustained power and usually a bare-tool price (no battery). If you already own a brand's batteries, a cordless saw on that platform is a easy add.

buyers_guide.q: What blade size do I need?
buyers_guide.a: 7-1/4 inch is the full-size standard — it cuts through 2x lumber in a single pass and is what most corded saws use. 6-1/2 inch is common on cordless saws: lighter, slightly shallower. 5-1/2 inch and smaller are compact saws for plywood, trim, and sheet goods, not framing.

buyers_guide.q: Amps vs volts — how much power?
buyers_guide.a: Corded saws are rated in amps; 15 amps is full power, 13 amps is a small step down that's fine for occasional use. Cordless saws are rated in volts (18V/20V MAX) — the battery and motor matter more than the number. Don't compare amps to volts directly.

A sidewinder (in-line) saw is lighter and cheaper, with the motor beside the blade — what most people should buy. A worm-drive saw gears the motor for more torque and a front-heavy balance pros like for rip cuts and wet lumber; heavier and pricier.

An electric brake stops the spinning blade in a second or two when you release the trigger, instead of letting it coast. It's a real safety and convenience feature — worth looking for, and one reason the DEWALT DWE575SB is our top all-around pick.
